Whether those checks are the right kind is §4.4’s question.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.4 Transformative experience

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Paul’s Transformative Experience formalises a problem the contemplative traditions have always faced without naming it. Some experiences are epistemically transformative: they provide knowledge of what an experience is like that was unavailable beforehand. They can also be personally transformative, changing preferences and values. Choosing whether to undergo such an experience challenges ordinary expected-value reasoning because relevant knowledge, and sometimes the values used to assess outcomes, emerge through the experience itself.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: This is precisely the structure of a call to practice. The darshan’s demand that understanding be conveyable before it is accepted is an attempt to escape it — to make the case in terms available to the unawakened. Paul’s analysis suggests why that is hard: if realisation changes what one values and how one understands experience, prior assessment may lack relevant knowledge while retrospective assessment reflects changed commitments. That asymmetry complicates appraisal without making every prior reason or later judgment worthless. Advaita’s qualification requirement (§2.2) approaches preparedness through disciplines that shape the learner’s disposition towards inquiry.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.5 Contemplative science and its reckoning

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Empirical work on meditation has identified measurable differences and has also undergone a methodological correction. Electroencephalography identified differences in gamma activity between long-term practitioners and controls during meditation and at baseline (Lutz et al. 2004). Such group differences alone do not isolate the causal contribution of training. Van Dam and colleagues’ “Mind the Hype” documented problems including inconsistent definitions, weak controls, small samples, and publication bias. Lindahl and colleagues catalogued difficult and sometimes destabilising experiences among Western Buddhist practitioners; their purposive sampling identifies kinds of difficulty rather than estimating prevalence. Thompson challenges the philosophical conclusions sometimes drawn from contemplative neuroscience (Thompson 2020).

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: The distinction relevant here is between evidence of change and evidence for the content of a resulting belief. Measures of attention, affect, or self-report do not by themselves establish that an ontology is true. Empirical inquiry can nevertheless test specified consequences of a claim, including accuracy, behaviour, and successful transmission. None of the studies cited here directly evaluates Madhyasth Darshan’s course of study or establishes its account of realisation.

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: 3.6 Method, evidence, and what modern work establishes

passages.heading: 3-modern-western-philosophy-and-contemplative-science
passages.section: 3. Modern Western Philosophy and Contemplative Science
passages.text: Modern philosophy establishes that transformation-oriented practice belongs to philosophy’s own history rather than outside it; that no description of a contemplative state settles whether its content is given or constructed; that the demand for cross-checking is reasonable but not obviously decisive against experiential justification; and that appraising transformative experience from outside is structurally difficult. Contemplative science establishes that practice has measurable effects, that the field’s early claims outran its methods, and that adverse effects are real. None of it establishes what realisation is or whether anyone has attained it.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4. Comparison

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.1 Criteria for comparison

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: The three positions are compared on eight questions: what the goal is; whether it is already present; what practice produces; what the decisive means is; the status of absorbed states; what counts as evidence of attainment; the place of conduct and relationship; and what liberation and the world afterwards are.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.2 Cross-tradition summary

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Modern philosophy and science The goal Realisation of existence as coexistence — of all units saturated in the omnipresent; liberation from delusion Moksha — recognition of what is eternally the case No settled goal; passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.3 The status of the absorbed state

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: This is where the comparison is most instructive, because the apparent clash is smaller than it looks and the real one is elsewhere. Nagraj’s report that his foundational questions remained unanswered in samadhi is not a refutation of Shankara, who holds that knowledge and not absorption removes ignorance. Their shared target is absorption taken by itself as sufficient for knowledge. Madhyasth Darshan still names accomplished realisation a state, kaivalya (§1.5). The report does reach an Advaita practice as Nagraj understood it, since he grouped nididhyasana with samadhi as states of thoughtlessness (AVD, p. 72); an Advaitin would reply that this is not what nididhyasana is.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: The genuine divergence is over what replaces the absorbed state. Advaita centres knowledge of the scriptural teaching, supported by reasoning and contemplation, and gives first-person knowledge and the characteristics of steady wisdom their respective roles. The darshan replaces it with study leading to definitive understanding and its satisfaction in realisation, and joins the intrinsic evidential standing of realisation to its public expression in conveyability, conduct, and experiment. Gupta’s account of nididhyasan names this unfolding towards establishment in coexistence, so the meaningful comparison concerns what becomes understood and established, rather than contemplation on one side and its absence on the other (RG). So the traditions agree in their negative diagnosis and in holding that the reality to be realised is already present, and differ over the authority of the teaching, the content realised, and the role of public evidence.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.4 What could count as a check

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: All three positions face the cross-checking problem and answer differently. Advaita gives first-person knowledge a role that is not made dependent on public ratification, while describing its characteristics in living (§2.6). Alston argues that demanding sense-perception-style checks of mystical practice begs the question. The darshan supplies observable expressions through which a claim to realisation can be checked, including more than conveyability: evidence in behaviour and in experiment with nature, a criterion of truth as what is uniformly realised by everyone, and the requirement that the reality each word names be found in existence (MVD, pp. 12, 35; AVD, pp. 61, 235).

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: These checks establish more than coherence. They test just conduct, successful work with nature, and agreement among those who have studied. What they test less directly is the ontology conveyed — the jeevan atom, the saturation of every unit in space — because a learner checks each claim against existence as the darshan’s own categories present it. Advaita’s first-person appeal does not itself resolve that difficulty for an outside observer. It is a reason to say that the darshan’s demand for evidence is a real advance in kind, whose force depends on how independent its checks are of the understanding they are meant to confirm (§6.3).

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.5 Transformation and the appraisal problem

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: Paul’s analysis (§3.4) applies unevenly across the three, and the unevenness is illuminating. Advaita approaches preparedness through the sadhana-chatushtaya, cultivating the dispositions required for inquiry. Hadot’s ancients handle it by making the exercises continuous with ordinary life, so each step is appraisable from the one before. Madhyasth Darshan takes the second route and pushes it further. It requires that understanding be conveyable to the unawakened at every stage, that each learner examine what is presented, and that belief follow knowing (MVD, p. 12; AVD, pp. 225–226), and it names marks of development in the learner’s own faculties — affection, peace, contentment, bliss — with defined content in understanding and conduct (MVD, pp. 282–283, 323–325, 327). These are its strongest anti-esoteric commitments.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: The residual difficulty is that the darshan also asks for full dedication in obedience to a realised teacher (MVD, p. 317) and holds that correct evaluation occurs only through awakening (MVD, p. 203; Axiology Value Theory §1.7). Those two commitments reintroduce from the other side the asymmetry conveyability was meant to remove.

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: 4.6 Practice as private or social

passages.heading: 4-comparison
passages.text: On this the darshan is the outlier, and it is a genuine contribution. Advaita’s path is compatible with solitude and its qualification list is a list of personal virtues. The empirical studies cited here primarily assess individual practitioners and outcomes. Here real upasana is behaving with one’s equal and practising towards greater awakening, and sociality is naturally contained in its results (KD, p. 37); upasana is education and orderliness in its own nature (KD, p. 42); and many of the 122 conducts it activates — kindness, grace, compassion, forgiveness, respect, affection, generosity — are directed to others (§1.9). Relationship enters the purpose, practice, and fulfilment of awakening. This commitment permits solitary reflection while requiring understanding to become effective in social living. Nagraj contrasts it with the samadhi pursuit he describes as preventing participation in family or society (AVD, p. 165). Hadot’s ancients are the nearest analogue — philosophy practised in the city, with the school as its setting — though even there the exercises are individual and the community supports them rather than constituting them.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5. Critical Review

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.1 Madhyasth Darshan — a demanding standard, resting on one report

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The distinction in §1.3 is transferable: the attainment of absorption does not by itself establish that the practitioner’s questions have been answered or their ontology verified.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: It is made from the inside, by a practitioner who reached the state he then declined to credit — which insulates it from the objection that critics of contemplative claims have not done the practice.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The refusal of ineffability is disciplined and consistent. Knowledge is held to be manifest and effable and its evidence accessible through behaviour, so the tradition produces statable doctrine open to examination.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The account of what practice changes is specific. The ten activities, the four and a half that are effective in delusion, and the 122 conducts of awakened jeevan give practice definite targets and definite marks, faculty by faculty. Gupta’s explanation further connects the learner’s listening and reasoning with practice in living and the unfolding into established understanding and realisation (RG).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Failure has stated conditions. Reflection fails in the presence of crime, injustice, attachment, or ignorance, and each has a named support; upasana fails when aim, seeker, and means come apart (MVD, p. 284; KD, p. 38).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Practice includes conduct in relationships as part of its fulfilment, so social obligation belongs within its account of awakening.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The traditional vocabulary of devotion and discipline is kept and given a public content rather than discarded, which lets the darshan meet those traditions on their own terms.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The dependency circle is stated in the darshan’s own words (MVD, p. 290) rather than concealed.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The founding exploration is available through one practitioner’s first-person report, including his design of the productive method (JV, p. 13). That historical episode cannot be independently repeated as the same event; the stated claims and proposed course of study remain open to examination.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The public marks test competence, conduct, and successful work more directly than they test the ontology conveyed (§§4.4, 6.3).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The texts pull in two directions on the teacher: dedicated obedience and adherence to instruction on one side, each learner’s examination and acceptance or rejection on the other (§6.4).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The inverted samadhi–dhyan–dharana sequence and its object, space, are reported, not argued. Why realisation should follow from them is not explained.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The printed passages and Gupta’s explanation specify the content and direction of practice, but leave its duration and the assessment of incomplete attainment less specified (§6.6). The treatise devoted to the systematic study of the 122 conducts is not yet available in translation.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan joins demanding criteria for understanding and conduct to a founding exploration known through testimony; assessing the transmission of its understanding is therefore central.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.2 Advaita Vedanta — knowledge and the characteristics of wisdom

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The argument that an eternally free self cannot be produced by action challenges accounts that make liberation a newly created condition.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Subordinating absorption to knowledge anticipates the darshan’s negative finding by more than a millennium.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The qualification structure is explicit about what a seeker must already possess rather than assuming availability on demand.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Shravana–manana–nididhyasana is a genuine account of how a knowledge event, not an experience, could remove ignorance.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: First-person knowledge and described characteristics do not by themselves provide an outside observer with a procedure for distinguishing realisation from confident self-ascription.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Dependence on sruti limits the argument’s reach to those who grant the source’s authority.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The internal dispute over samadhi between Shankara and later texts is unresolved, which weakens appeals to “the Advaita position” on practice.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita gives a developed argument for liberation through knowledge of an already free self, while leaving the public adjudication of another person’s attainment less specified than the disciplines and characteristics of the knower.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.3 Modern philosophy and science — clear questions, differing accounts of the goal

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Hadot recovered transformation-oriented practice as philosophy’s own history, which reframes the whole subject.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The perennialist–constructivist dispute isolates exactly the question that first-person reports cannot settle.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Alston forces critics to state why cross-checking should be required rather than assuming it.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Paul’s analysis explains why transformative practice can be difficult to appraise from present knowledge and values.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Contemplative science has corrected itself in public — “Mind the Hype” and the adverse-effects literature are the field policing its own claims.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: No convergence on whether contemplative states can justify belief, and each position’s answer follows from prior commitments.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The cited measurements of change do not by themselves establish the truth of contemplative claims; that requires tests directed at the particular content claimed.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The literature is overwhelmingly built on Buddhist-derived and theistic practices, so its categories fit a darshan that rejects absorption as a goal and rebuilds devotion around understanding rather poorly.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Modern philosophy and science clarify the problems of interpretation, justification, transformation, and measurement, without supplying a settled account of realisation shared across these approaches.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6. Open problems for Madhyasth Darshan

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.1 The inverted sequence

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The samadhi–dhyan–dharana order is given as the process for samyama (MVD, p. 7), undertaken to test samadhi (JV, p. 13) and directed at space (AVD, p. 72), without any statement of why that order on that object should work. Three readings are possible: that the absorbed state quiets the sensory circuit so directed attention can operate without interference; that the descent is incidental and the work was done by sustained attention regardless of order; or that the sequence records one person’s route without general significance. The darshan’s own vocabulary suggests a fourth. If dhyan is concentration for understanding (MVD, p. 284) and dharana is innateness (MVD, p. 43), the sequence would run from the silence of the faculties, through concentration for understanding, to the apprehension of each thing’s innateness in the space that saturates it. That reading is not stated in the texts reviewed, and none of the four is argued there.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.2 Entry into the circle

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The dependency passage concerns the ability for realisation in knowledge, awakening, sanskar, environment, study, and humaneness (MVD, p. 290). Following, emulation, and study provide a stated path (MVD, pp. 280–282), outward expressions of values can be learnt before establishment in state, and belief may precede knowing provided knowing follows (MVD, p. 12). These supply an entry into learning, and the printed texts recommend study with inquiry as the practicable route without requiring every learner to repeat the founder’s exploration (AVD, pp. 72–74, 225).

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The remaining question concerns warrant and transmission. The system studied originates in the founder’s exploration, and the exploratory route is not recommended to others. A public account should therefore show how learners can examine the teaching, identify an error in its presentation or application, and verify their progress through understanding and conduct. The texts supply the criterion that each person examine and accept or reject what is presented (AVD, p. 226), but they do not describe a procedure by which a community of learners corrects a teacher’s presentation.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.3 What the evidential marks establish

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The darshan’s evidential marks are richer than conveyability: realisation, behaviour, and experiment (MVD, p. 12); the absence of mistakes and crimes in behaviour (MVD, p. 285); the ability to provide justice (AVD, pp. 172–173); truth as what is uniformly realised by everyone (MVD, p. 35; AVD, p. 61); and the requirement that the reality each word names be found in existence (AVD, p. 235). Each tests something real. Conveyability tests coherence and pedagogical competence, conduct tests whether the understanding governs living, and experiment tests whether it succeeds in work with nature.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The difficulty lies in what they are meant to confirm. Praman is the fourth stage of the same sequence as sakshatkar (§1.11), so the marks are presented as consequences of realisation. They also provide observers with grounds for assessing a claim to it. Conduct and successful work are compatible with an understanding whose ontology is mistaken, since people live justly and produce well on many metaphysics. Finding each named reality in existence presupposes that existence is presented in the darshan’s categories. And agreement among learners trained in one system is not independent confirmation of that system, as the constructivist argument of §3.2 would predict. What would settle the question is a check on the content of sakshatkar that does not already rely on the understanding sakshatkar is supposed to deliver. The automaticity claimed in §1.11 concerns successful sakshatkar, so it does not imply that a mistaken self-ascription would produce its fruits. The diagnostic question is how a learner or observer distinguishes successful recognition from confident fluency and partial changes in conduct before the full criteria are met.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The darshan’s strongest reply is the invariance criterion. If realisation is the same in all who reach it and is of what is uniformly present everywhere, divergent realisations would expose error. That reply needs a public record of independent realisers whose accounts can be compared, and the texts reviewed do not provide one.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.4 The teacher and the learner’s own examination

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The texts pull in two directions. On one side, realisation requires full dedication in obedience to a realised human being (MVD, p. 317), and dharma can be realised only through study and adherence to the step-by-step instructions of one who has attained realisation (MVD, p. 273). On the other, each person examines any presentation and accepts or rejects it (AVD, p. 226); a tradition’s commands remain information until they become studiable in logic and behaviour (AVD, p. 225); instruction by sermon risks delusion (AVD, p. 225); and belief is to follow knowing (MVD, p. 12). These are consistent if the teacher’s instructions govern the conduct of study while their content is established only by the learner’s own examination and conduct. The texts do not say this in so many words, and the practical difficulty remains that a student cannot certify a teacher as realised without the understanding the teacher is supposed to impart.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: Nagraj’s recorded remarks point the same way. He describes his own presentation as proceeding by goodwill and friendship, with no dadagiri — no bullying — the bullying in question being the older way of saying “you will ask nothing” (26:50). He treats self-examination as the test of teaching, asking whether one says, does, and lives the same thing (31:15–32:48), and of his critical method he says that he reviewed ideas and did not go about reviewing persons (41:14). Read provisionally, these remarks favour examination rather than coercion. The goodwill passage still requires an audio check, so it does not independently resolve the relationship between the printed requirements of dedication and examination.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.5 How failure is diagnosed

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The texts state the conditions under which the practice fails. Reflection fails when crime, injustice, attachment, or ignorance is present and its corresponding support — orderliness, social conduct, study and sanskar, inward regulation — is absent (MVD, p. 284); upasana fails when aim, seeker, and means are separated (KD, p. 38); and humans decline, while wanting awakening, for lack of understanding of the reflection and projection among their own faculties (MVD, p. 291). What is not stated is how these conditions are to be read from outside in a particular learner, how long a successful course of study takes, or what a practitioner should conclude from years of study without sakshatkar.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The provisional claim of automatic succession in the recorded session sharpens the gap. If bodh, anubhav, and praman follow once sakshatkar succeeds (03:03), a failure downstream calls into question either the diagnosis of successful sakshatkar or the claimed automatic succession. The printed conditions of reflection identify possible failures in the relations between faculties. The account also places responsibility for successful study on teachers, guardians, teaching, and educational content and procedure together (MVD, p. 270). Failure therefore calls for examination of the learning conditions as well as the learner. The material reviewed does not supply a documented series of unsuccessful courses of study and their diagnoses against which the proposed conditions could be tested.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.6 The detail of practice

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: For a study of spiritual practice the corpus contains more procedural content than a first reading suggests: the two programmes of the second path (MVD, p. 282), the four supports of reflection (MVD, p. 284), concentration for understanding (MVD, p. 284), the marks of each faculty’s development (MVD, pp. 282–283, 322–323, 327), the refinement of the fundamental tendencies through upasana and restraint (KD, pp. 30–40), and the inventory of 122 conducts (§1.9). Its central instruction is study, including listening, reflection, and understanding meaning (MVD, p. 257), and the recorded session names sakshatkar as study succeeding (12:54). Focused contemplative attention also has an explicit place: dhyan is concentration for understanding meaning and evidencing it (MVD, pp. 284–285).

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: Gupta’s explanation adds a connected account of the learner’s work: listening with the intention to understand, ratiocination that joins different threads into a coherent view and conclusions for living, and nididhyasan as the unfolding into direct cognition, conception and resolve, realisation, and indelible establishment as sanskar (RG). It supplies a developmental direction without separating listening and reasoning into non-overlapping periods.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: Together these sources identify learner activities, conditions, developmental relations, and responsibilities. What remains less specified is a curriculum with durations and independently applicable milestones: the depth of study needed by a particular learner, how partial progress towards establishment is assessed, and how unsuccessful teaching or study is corrected. The treatise the darshan names for the systematic study of the awakened conducts, Manav Sanchetnavadi Manovigyan (AVD, p. 151), may supply part of this, but it has not yet been translated in this collection.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.7 Adverse effects

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: The contemplative-science literature documents reported difficulties associated with practice (§3.5), and Nagraj’s own regime of twelve to eighteen hours daily for years (MVD, p. 7) is intensive by any standard. The darshan does caution against the route he took: the method of silence is against the natural manifestation of jeevan (AVD, p. 74), it leaves the practitioner without a programme of living and unable to take part in family and society (AVD, pp. 164–165, 220), and the tradition’s own stories of bodies becoming inactive in samadhi are noted (AVD, p. 164). For its own recommended route it makes a strong claim: the progress of awakening involves no pain, and all pain belongs to wrongful activity and decline (KD, p. 36). The Buddhist-practice findings do not directly test the Madhyasth route, and their sampling does not establish a rate of harm. The darshan’s own claim calls for evidence from its course of study: how difficulties are identified, whether they arise, and how teachers and learners respond.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: 6.8 Translation and source coverage

passages.heading: 6-open-problems-for-madhyasth-darshan
passages.text: Much of the positive account rests on material available here only in working translation. The upasana chapter of Manav Karm Darshan is a machine-assisted working translation; for this study its key passages were compared with the Hindi source pages and found to support the readings used (Editorial Notes). The English of Adhyatmvad, the darshan’s own treatment of spirituality, is a work-in-progress translation not yet peer reviewed, and Manav Sanchetnavadi Manovigyan, the treatise on the 122 conducts, has not been translated. The account of liberation, of study as practice, and of the activation of the faculties should be rechecked as those translations mature.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: 7. Conclusion

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s account of practice is organised around a refusal. Its founder pursued the method he was told was the only way to know the unknown, reached the state it aims at, and reported that knowing the unknown did not occur: his foundational questions remained unanswered and he could not present evidence of the attainment. What replaces it is not a sparse residue but a full positive account. Spirituality is the understanding of the omnipresent reality in which every unit is saturated, and its accomplishment is atma-bodh together with realisation in coexistence. Realisation is the satisfaction of a definitive understanding of existence, jeevan, and humane conduct, and it is evidenced in behaviour, experiment, and tradition. Practice is study — overlapping listening and ratiocination, accompanied by practice in living — together with refinement of the fundamental tendencies, inward regulation of the faculties, and concentration for understanding and evidence. Gupta describes nididhyasan as the unfolding through direct cognition, conception and resolve, and realisation, becoming established in coexistence as an indelible impression in jeevan (RG). What practice aims at is the awakening of all ten activities of jeevan, of which only four and a half are effective in delusion, and their evidence in 122 conducts that include devotion, reverence, love, forgiveness, gratitude, and restraint. The traditional vocabulary of devotion, discipline, and liberation — bhakti, dhyan, yog, vairagya, jeevan-mukta, kaivalya — is kept and redefined by understanding and conduct. What is rejected is the path of mystery, faith without knowing, renunciation as an ideal, and the absorbed state as a goal.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: Against Advaita the disagreement is narrower and deeper than it first appears. Both hold that the reality to be realised is already present, and both distinguish knowledge from the mere attainment of absorption; Shankara’s subordination of absorption to knowledge anticipates the darshan’s negative finding. They part on what the self and the world are — Brahman and mithya against a finite jeevan saturated in the omnipresent and a perpetual world — on what does the work of knowing, and on whether realisation owes anyone public evidence. Advaita joins first-person knowledge with described characteristics of steady wisdom. Madhyasth Darshan makes conveyance, work, conduct, and continuity in tradition integral to its account of evidence.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: Modern philosophy turns out to have a great deal to say. Hadot shows that transformation-oriented practice is philosophy’s own inheritance rather than something outside it. The perennialist–constructivist dispute shows that the founder’s report of a silent state can be read as evidence for either view, which is a caution about how much any such report can settle. Alston shows that the demand for cross-checking needs defending rather than assuming. Paul explains why transformative practice complicates appraisal from present knowledge and values — the difficulty the darshan’s conveyability requirement is designed to escape and does not entirely escape. And contemplative science distinguishes measurable differences and reported changes from the further tests needed to assess a claim to knowledge.

passages.heading: 7-conclusion
passages.text: The darshan’s transferable contribution is the demand to distinguish contemplative attainment from what that attainment establishes. Nagraj makes the distinction from within the practice he pursued; its force lies in asking what has been understood and how that understanding becomes evident. Its positive account is more specific than a first reading suggests, since it names the faculties practice must activate, the conditions under which each step succeeds or fails, and the conducts by which awakening is to be recognised. Its cost is that its public marks test conduct and competence more directly than the ontology they are meant to confirm, that the teacher’s authority and the learner’s own examination stand in tension, and that its positive foundation rests on a single report and a method its author devised for himself. A reader who wants to test the darshan should test it where it asks to be tested: in whether study of its stated system brings the faculties into the order it describes, and whether the conduct that follows is the conduct it predicts.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §1

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Adhyatma — spirit; the darshan’s name for the omnipresent reality in which all units are saturated, from which anubhavatmak adhyatmvad, realisation-centred spiritualism, takes its name (AVD, pp. 235–236). The spiritual aspect of existence, as distinct from the deific (intellectual) and the metaphysical (insentient) (MVD, p. 285).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Atma-bodh — enlightenment of the self; the spiritual accomplishment, reached through inward regulation and coming into effect together with Brahma-realisation, realisation in coexistence (MVD, pp. 283, 286).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Sakshatkar — direct recognition, in chitta (MVD, p. 126); also rendered “revelation” (JV, p. 62). On oral testimony, the success of study (§1.11).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bodh — enlightenment; affirmation in buddhi through study (MVD, p. 126); complete bodh coincides with anubhav in atma (MVD, p. 207).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Avdharana — definitive understanding: knowing, believing, and recognising (AVD, p. 224).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Anubhav — realisation. Realisation in the ultimate truth which is in the form of coexistence (MVD, p. 316), an activity of atma; attaining the point of satisfaction in definitive understanding (AVD, p. 224). In the recorded session, also called drashtapad, the seat of the seer (§1.11).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Praman — evidence; the fourth stage. Evidence is threefold — realisation, behaviour, experiment — and evidence is awakened tradition (MVD, p. 12). Its expression in conduct and orderliness is authenticity (pramanikta) (AVD, p. 224).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Tadroop, tadakar, tatsannidhya, tadavalokan — absolute-accordance, absolute-resonance, absolute-connectedness, and absolute-observance with the ideal; the goals of pursuing the ideal, reached through realisation in coexistence. Tadavalokan is establishment in the seer status in coexistence, and the tat- prefix denotes awakening (MVD, p. 80).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Ishta — the ideal: self-driven reverence, trust, and dedication towards coexistence together with complete knowledge (MVD, p. 80); awakening is the human ideal (MVD, pp. 306–307).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bal, shakti — the inexhaustible strengths (mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi, atma) and powers (hope, thought, desire, resoluteness, authenticity) of jeevan (MVD, pp. 75, 275; AVD, p. 151).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Ten activities — taste and selection (mun), deliberation and analysis (vritti), contemplation and visualisation (chitta), enlightenment and resolve (buddhi), realisation and authenticity (atma) (JV, pp. 73, 92–93).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Four and a half activities — the activities effective in delusion: selection, taste, analysis, visualisation, and deliberation confined to the pleasant, healthy, and profitable (JV, p. 73; AVD, p. 152).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: 122 conducts — the detailed activities of awakened jeevan: two in atma, four in buddhi, sixteen in chitta, thirty-six in vritti, and sixty-four in mun (MVD, p. 323; AVD, p. 91).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Ritambhara — resoluteness; the entire backdrop for the manifestation of the natural grandeur of truth, a resolve suffused with truth; distinct from sankalp, resolve (MVD, p. 76).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Antarniyaman — inward regulation of jeevan’s powers, required for the reception of higher-conformance signals and for atma-bodh (MVD, pp. 77, 283–286).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Dhyan — concentration: focusing mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi for understanding, and for evidence after understanding and realisation (MVD, p. 284).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Shravan, manan, arth-bodh — listening, ratiocination, and understanding meaning in teacher-guided study (MVD, p. 257). Gupta explains shravan and manan as overlapping: listening aims at understanding meaning; ratiocination draws its different threads into a coherent view and conclusions for living, accompanied by practice (RG).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Manan, tulan — in the faculty correspondence, affirmation through acceptance in mun and qualitative deliberation in vritti, respectively (MVD, p. 126); manan also receives the justice-based thought of vritti (MVD, p. 295). The method-level use of manan as ratiocination is broader than this particular correspondence.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Nididhyasan — in Gupta’s explanation, the unfolding of direct cognition (sakshatkar), conception in buddhi and resolve, and thereafter realisation in atma: becoming established in the understanding and realisation of coexistence as an indelible impression in jeevan (RG).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Sanskar — formation developed through study, behaviour, and work (MVD, pp. 187, 218, 290); in fulfilled nididhyasan, the indelible impression of understood and realised coexistence in jeevan (RG).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Shruti — realised articulation: giving language to understanding and communicating realities in coexistence (MVD, pp. 324, 329). Distinct from shravan, listening.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Shanti, santosh, anand — peace as behaviour based on resolved thought; contentment as absence of the sentiment of lacking; bliss as complete enlightenment of mediative activity or atma-bodh (MVD, pp. 323–325).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Gyan-anubhuti ki yogyata — ability for realisation in knowledge, which develops in mutual dependence with awakening, formation, environment, study, endeavour, and humaneness (MVD, p. 290).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bhas, abhas, prateeti — perception, comprehension, and awareness of realisation, where vritti meets mun, chitta meets vritti, and buddhi meets chitta (MVD, p. 99).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Anusandhan — exploration; the first of the two paths, the route of a seeker accomplished in samadhi (MVD, pp. 280–281).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Gyan-anubhuti — realisation in knowledge; the same realisation considered as the knowing of coexistence (MVD, pp. 290, 316).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Rahasya — mystery. Not revealing understanding, not being able to, or not being able to attain it (MVD, p. 273); incompleteness in understanding the absolute state and activity (MVD, p. 209).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bhram — delusion: belief different from reality (MVD, p. 291). Its bondage is threefold, of hope, thought, and desire (AVD, pp. 155, 167).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Ahankar — ego: buddhi without atma-bodh, appearing as conceit in chitta, stubbornness in vritti, and attachment and agitation in mun (MVD, p. 279).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bhram-mukti — liberation from delusion; the darshan’s proposal for liberation (MVD, p. 149), identified with seedless thought and behaviour (MVD, p. 81). Freedom from the bondage of delusion is moksha (AVD, p. 84).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Jeevan-mukta — one liberated from animal consciousness and delusion while living, free of suffering over past and future, whose essential nature is nurturing society (MVD, pp. 81, 157).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Kaivalya — absoluteness; the state of realisation, with liberation from suffering, resentment, fear, and the bondage of delusion (MVD, pp. 317–318), evidenced as participation in the whole of orderliness (AVD, pp. 260–261).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Samadhi — reported by Nagraj as the state in which hope, thought, and desire fall silent while knowing the unknown does not occur (MVD, p. 7; JV, p. 13); self-limited happiness (svantah sukh) (AVD, p. 220).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Samyama — the method Nagraj devised after rejecting Patanjali’s, run as samadhi, dhyan, dharana and directed at space (MVD, p. 7; JV, p. 13; AVD, p. 72); also, as one of the 122 conducts, restraint: being regulated in humane thought, behaviour, and vocation (MVD, p. 337).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Dharana — in this darshan’s definitions, innateness, that which cannot be separated from a thing (MVD, p. 43).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Dharma — a unit’s innateness; human dharma is happiness, expressed through resolved thought and participation in orderliness (MVD, pp. 51, 156, 174).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Upasana — the refining and transforming of the fundamental tendencies, and itself a form of study (KD, pp. 30, 38); education and orderliness in its own nature (KD, p. 42); of three kinds, kutastha, rupastha, and atmastha (KD, p. 31).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Sadhana — effort towards self-improvement, whose point of fulfilment is awakening (AVD, pp. 233–234).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Abhyas — practice: carrying the awakening attained into behaviour and teaching as comprehensive resolution (AVD, p. 234).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Bhakti — devotion: the activity of becoming liberated from fear and delusion, the expression of prayer joined with seva, and an expression of total dedication (MVD, p. 339).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Par-vairagya — supreme detachment: liberation from the flaws of excess, deficiency, and omission that stand against awakening (MVD, pp. 157–158).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Yog — union, of two kinds, unification and togetherness (MVD, p. 42); pre-existing yog, the union with the omnipresent that is only realised, and attainable yog, the unions a unit enters (MVD, pp. 159, 302).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Prayog — experimentation: the endeavour, continued until it succeeds, to instil usefulness and aesthetic value in natural abundance (MVD, p. 56).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Chintan — contemplation. The awareness of truth (MVD, p. 316); the strength with which awakening begins (AVD, p. 151).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Realisation-oriented way (anubhav-gami vidhi) — practice that regulates hope, thought, and desire in relation to the resolve towards realisation in atma (MVD, p. 277).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Realisation-based way (anubhav-moolak vidhi) — the mode in which an awakened jeevan evidences all ten of its activities, and in which teaching is conducted; realisation is expressed through enlightenment, contemplation, deliberation, and the taste of values (MVD, pp. 79, 99, 276–277).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Integrality — justice, dharma, and truth-based behaviour, thought, and realisation together (MVD, p. 303).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §2

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Moksha — liberation; eternally accomplished and obscured by ignorance rather than produced.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Avidya — ignorance, whose removal is liberation.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Adhyasa — superimposition of self and not-self, the subject of Shankara’s preamble to the Brahma Sutra Bhashya.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Sadhana-chatushtaya — the fourfold qualification: viveka, vairagya, the six treasures, mumukshutva.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Shravana, manana, nididhyasana — hearing, reasoning, and sustained contemplation.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Turiya — the fourth state, beyond waking, dream, and deep sleep (MU, vv. 3–7).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Jivanmukta — one liberated while living; the characteristics of steady wisdom describe the knower and guide the seeker (BG 2.54–72).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Loka-sangraha — the holding-together of the world; the ground of continued action (BG 3.20, 3.25–26).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §3

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Spiritual exercises — Hadot’s term for the transformative practices of ancient philosophy.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Askesis — training or discipline of the self; Foucault’s care of the self.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Perennialism — the view that mystical experience has a common core across traditions (Stace).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Constructivism — the view that tradition-specific concepts shape the experience itself, not only its report (Katz).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Pure consciousness event — a contentless state of awareness, defended by Forman.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Mystical perceptual practice — Alston’s term for the doxastic practice of forming beliefs from experience of God.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Epistemically transformative experience — an experience that supplies previously unavailable knowledge of what it is like; personal transformation concerns changes in values and preferences (Paul).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The founder’s report as evidence

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: §§1.3–1.4 rest on autobiographical passages in MVD, JV, and AVD. This study treats them as first-person historical testimony about how the darshan arose — evidence of the reported route, without independently establishing either the ontology realised or its reproducibility — and says so in §1.16 and §5.1 rather than letting them function as demonstration. The Epistemology study takes the same line at its §1.6.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Recorded oral teaching as a source

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: §§1.11, 1.12, 6.4, 6.5, and 6.6 draw on a recorded session of January 2010 at Amarkantak, Sakshatkar – Bodh – Anubhav – Praman, under four constraints. It never outweighs a printed text; where the two differ the text governs. It is cited by timestamp, so a reader can tell at a glance which claims rest on it. It is machine-transcribed Hindi that no Hindi speaker has yet checked against the audio, and the transcript records per-segment which passages are secure. And it is occasion-bound teaching, answering the people in the room rather than composed for publication.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The printed definitions establish realisation as the point of satisfaction in definitive understanding (AVD, p. 224) and give reasons for preferring the practicable study route (AVD, pp. 72–74, 225). They are related to, but do not verify, the transcript’s stronger statements that anubhav adds no content beyond what sakshatkar makes firm (22:28) and that exploration is impractical for all (34:07). The transcript explicitly reserves these passages, and the assertion that there is no other method (14:12), for audio verification before released reliance. §§1.11–1.12 therefore rest their corresponding claims on the printed formulations.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The names drashtapad for anubhav and jagriti for praman (13:09, 17:30, 21:13), and the automatic succession of stages after sakshatkar (03:03–03:30), were not located in the printed passages reviewed. They remain attributed to the working transcript, and §6.5 examines automaticity conditionally. Form, property, and essential nature can be understood while dharma can only be realised (MVD, p. 273), so the printed account should not be reduced to an idle repetition of recognition. The goodwill-versus-coercion passage (26:50) used in §6.4 also remains provisionally transcribed; it cannot independently settle the teacher-authority question. The transcript, translation, and per-segment reliability marks are published as Sakshatkar – Bodh – Anubhav – Praman (2010, Amarkantak); the analysis behind these sections is in the companion research note alongside this file.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Study functions and developmental order

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD p. 257 names shravan, manan, and arth-bodh as elements of successful teacher-guided study. P. 126 maps affirmation of coexistence to manan in mun, tulan in vritti, sakshatkar in chitta, and bodh in buddhi. It does not prescribe completing manan before beginning tulan. P. 295 also describes manan as receiving justice-based thought from vritti. §§1.6 and 1.11 therefore distinguish the learner’s activities, faculty correspondences, and developmental direction. The ordered account in JV p. 62 is retained together with the explicit concurrence of complete bodh and anubhav (MVD, pp. 207, 286–287).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: This study uses manan as ratiocination in the account of the learner’s method, following Gupta’s explanation: coherent synthesis and logical conclusions about reality and living, accompanied by practice. MVD p. 126’s acceptance-related manan in mun is retained as a narrower faculty correspondence. The relation between these uses should not be compressed into either a compulsory manan–tulan timetable or a definition of all ratiocination as acceptance alone. Shravan, listening, is distinct from shruti, articulation of understanding (MVD, pp. 324, 329).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Gupta’s explanation of the method

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Rakesh Gupta’s explanation was supplied for this study on September 27, 2026. It is adopted here as a translator’s interpretation of the teaching method, separately attributed from Nagraj’s printed works and the 2010 recording. The supplied wording is:

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: shravan and manan overlap. shravan is listening with the intent of understanding the meaning. manan is ratiocination. it requires one to build a coherent view from different threads of listening and reach the logical conclusion about the way reality is, and how one should live therefore. it is accompanied with practice in living. nidhidhyasan is the unfolding of the direct-cognition (sakshatkar), conception in buddhi and resolve, and thereafter realisation in atma. It is to become established with the understanding (samajh) and realisation (anubhav) of coexistence, which gets instilled in jeevan as indelible impression (sanskar). — RG

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The date records when the explanation was supplied for this study, not when Gupta originally stated it. The quotation retains the supplied spelling nidhidhyasan; analytical prose uses nididhyasan. Its direction from cognition through conception and resolve to realisation is preserved alongside the printed statement that complete bodh and anubhav become effective together (MVD, pp. 207, 286–287). No separately timed interval between their completed forms is asserted. The indelibility in Gupta’s explanation concerns accomplished establishment in understanding and realisation; formative conceptions remain open to refinement through study and living (MVD, pp. 187, 218).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: AVD pp. 71–72 uses nididhyasan in Nagraj’s retrospective description of inherited prescriptions. Gupta supplies the positive teaching-method sense used in §§1.6 and 1.11; it is not attributed to that historical passage. Likewise, the comparison with BU 2.4.5 concerns becoming established through meaningful understanding, while keeping the respective accounts of self, reality, and fulfilment distinct (§2.3).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Tadroop-tadakar and the seer status

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The definition of tadroop-tadakar vidhi on MVD p. 80 belongs to the account of pursuing the ideal (ishta-sevan), whose four goals are oneness, accordance, abiding near, and continuous observance; establishment in the seer status is given there as the definition of the last of these, tadavalokan. This study therefore reads the sentence “Realisation in coexistence itself is the way of absolute-accordance and absolute-resonance” as the darshan’s reinterpretation of devotional union with a chosen ideal, not as a general thesis that method and realisation are identical, and it cites the recorded session rather than p. 80 for naming anubhav as drashtapad.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Samadhi in three vocabularies

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Samadhi names different things in the three traditions compared here, and this study does not harmonise them. In MVD, JV, and AVD it is the state Nagraj attained without resolving his foundational questions, and in which mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi have no remaining motion. In Advaita its status is internally disputed, subordinated to knowledge by Shankara and praised in later texts. In the modern literature it is one of several terms for absorption, with no settled referent across studies. Where §4.3 speaks of “the absorbed state”, that is this study’s neutral term and not a translation of any of the three.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Samyama, dharana, and dhyan

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Samyama appears in two senses: the method of §1.4, and restraint in humane thought, behaviour, and vocation as one of the 122 conducts (MVD, p. 337). §1.4 glosses the reversed sequence in the received sense of its terms and notes that the darshan’s own definitions give dharana as innateness (MVD, p. 43) and dhyan as concentration for understanding (MVD, p. 284). Whether those definitions apply to the words in the autobiographical passage is not stated in the texts reviewed; §6.1 records the reading they suggest without adopting it.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Sadhana, upasana, and the practice vocabulary

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The darshan keeps and redefines the traditional names of practice rather than replacing them (§1.8). MVD and JV use sadhana for the practice Nagraj pursued and moved beyond, while AVD redefines it as effort towards self-improvement whose fulfilment is awakening (AVD, pp. 233–234). This study uses sadhana in that redefined sense where AVD is under discussion, and otherwise prefers study, upasana, and practice for the darshan’s recommended course. Upasana is used in its redefined sense, with the traditional sense reported where the sources report it (MVD, p. 4; JV, p. 9). The same convention is followed in Family Relationships and Values.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Moksha and kaivalya

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: AVD defines moksha as freedom from the bondage of delusion and evidence of awakening (p. 84), and again places moksha in awakening (p. 167). Yet its account of kaivalya says that absoluteness lies in awakening “and not in moksha” (pp. 260–261). These passages do not establish two successive achievements called liberation and its positive completion. The contrast may address an inherited use of moksha, but the material reviewed does not settle that interpretation. §1.5 retains the supported positive account of freedom from delusion, realisation, and participation in orderliness; the unexplained contrast remains a textual question.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The 122 activities and their inventory

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: §1.9 names representative pairs from the 122 activities. The translation renders the members of several pairs differently in different places, and §1.9 follows MVD’s definitions — devotedness for anurag, devoutness for pujyata, and fearlessness for dhruti, defined as the absence of fear (MVD, p. 324). The complete tabulation, its bal–shakti assignments, and the points at which the tabulated assignment and the definitions diverge are recorded in The Sixty-One Activity Pairs of Jeevan; this study does not depend on resolving those points.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Working translations and page conventions

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD page numbers follow the printed page footers of the bilingual edition; where a Hindi passage and its English translation fall on facing pages, the page of the English is cited. The upasana chapter of Manav Karm Darshan is available here as a machine-assisted working translation. For this study the Hindi of KD printed pp. 30, 35, 36, 37, and 42 was compared with the rendered source pages and supports the translation at the points used. On p. 37 the Hindi reads जिसमें सामाजिकता स्वाभाविक रूप से समाहित रहती है, whose relative most naturally attaches to the direct fruit of upasana rather than to upasana itself; the same page defines real upasana as behaving with one’s equal and practising towards greater awakening, which supports §1.7’s relational purpose and fulfilment of practice, without excluding solitary reflection. AVD is cited from the page numbers of Sanjeev Chopra’s bilingual working translation (2023 edition), which has not yet been peer reviewed. Manav Sanchetnavadi Manovigyan has no English translation in this collection.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Modern sources selected for relevance, not coverage

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: §3 does not survey the philosophy of religion or the psychology of meditation. It selects the four bodies of work that bear on claims made in §1 — practice as philosophy, the content of contemplative states, the justification of experiential belief, and the appraisal of transformative experience — together with the methodological correction in contemplative science. Fuller treatment of religious experience and divinity belongs to God, Divinity, and the Sacred.
